title: Hikyo manages Hikyo
status: Expanded implementation built locally; acceptance and delivery remain open

explicit: Apply from Hikyo UI without restarting the container.
Require instance-admin access for system configuration changes.
Independent remote instances use separate configuration projects; only HA replicas of the same logical instance share configuration.
D11: every Hikyo variable, with remote Apply; only the target instance administrator with passkey or TOTP authentication may apply it.
Allow controlled bootstrap rollouts when startup inputs require them; ordinary settings reload live.
authority.delegation: I trust your instincts, assume I agree with the coming recommendations.
authority.scope: Remaining decisions selected under user-delegated authority. These are design decisions, not individual user answers or shipped behavior.

decisions.question: How should configuration changes take effect?
options: Apply from Hikyo
Activate a published revision from the UI without restarting the container.
Restart the service
Save values now and restart the process later.
Apply on every edit
Every draft edit immediately changes running behavior.
decisions.recommendation: Apply from Hikyo.
decisions.rationale: You explicitly chose UI application. A visible activation step makes the effective change deliberate and reviewable.
decisions.decision: Keep Edit, Publish and Apply separate. Apply configuration is an instance-admin action. A browser refresh never activates changes.
decisions.acceptance: A browser-only email change reaches the live mail client without changing the process start time.

decisions.question: Should Hikyo use its normal interface or a separate settings store?
options: Normal project and matrix
Reuse keys, schemas, drafts, publication, secret handling and history.
Separate settings forms and table
Build a second configuration system.
Mirror environment variables
Display settings but continue reading only the process environment.
decisions.recommendation: A real project, using the normal matrix.
decisions.rationale: Dogfooding should exercise the same storage and workflow that users rely on, with a small instance activation adapter.
decisions.decision: Each logical instance owns a real protected organization Hikyo, one project named for that instance and an active Production environment. A unified Hikyo root management view groups the local project and references to independently hosted remote projects. Instance settings opens the selected owner’s matrix and its own active/pending revision. A mail setup helper writes that project’s keys and drafts; it does not own another store. A remote is not another environment or node of the local project.
decisions.acceptance: Editing SMTP through either entry point changes the same owning project. Editing a remote instance never changes the local project or another remote.

decisions.question: When are the system resources created?
options: During initial setup
Provision after the first administrator exists and the keyring is initialized.
On every server start
Recreate or reseed resources on startup.
Manual organization creation
Ask the operator to prepare the hierarchy.
decisions.recommendation: Idempotent provisioning during initial setup.
decisions.rationale: Setup should leave Hikyo ready to manage itself without allowing subsequent startups to overwrite operator changes.
decisions.decision: A setup coordinator waits for the first administrator, then atomically creates the bound hierarchy, schema, explicit scoped grants, initial validated snapshot and active pointer using the server's effective configuration. Serialize concurrent coordinators. Until this transaction succeeds, setup remains incomplete with a named retryable error; do not fabricate a successful system project. Preserve the existing admin establishment ceremony. Provision per logical instance identity, not per server process, hostname, remote connection or HA node. Independent remotes run their own local setup; adding a remote does not seed it from the viewer’s variables. Host administrator creation must consume a fresh sealed owner/node seed from the running server, never evaluate its CLI environment as runtime authority. Missing or stale evidence refuses before principal creation and instructs starting the server before retrying. The sealed-seed import now has local both-engine authority/size and real app-listener regression evidence. R1 findings were fixed: final membership-locked verification preserves host discovery and reads a fresh decision clock. Both-engine regressions passed in 5.308 s; R2 review is clean for these fixes.
decisions.acceptance: Parallel HA starts create exactly one local binding; independent instances get distinct projects. Failed provisioning leaves no partial hierarchy; restarting preserves edited values.

decisions.question: How do existing installations adopt managed configuration?
options: Explicit one-time adoption
Preview supported settings, then seed without changing their effective values.
Automatic migration of all values
Transfer configuration as a side effect of upgrading.
Only support new installations
Leave existing operators on external configuration.
decisions.recommendation: One-time adoption from instance settings.
decisions.rationale: Existing installations should gain the feature without an upgrade silently changing configuration authority.
decisions.decision: Require instance administration and fresh reauthentication. Import only the current server's allowlisted effective settings. The adoption transaction is idempotent and uses the same provisioning service as fresh setup. In HA, every admitted node must attest equal canonical config using a secret-safe keyed comparison; differences block adoption by key name. Preserve the operator's existing environment files. Report name collisions; create an isolated suffixed system organization such as Hikyo System 2 without taking ownership of an existing tenant. Equality checks apply only to HA replicas sharing one logical instance. Never compare, synchronize or require equal variables across remote instances. Remote adoption runs on the owning instance through the human workspace session, using that owner’s effective config.
decisions.acceptance: Adoption retains behavior, handles collisions, refuses divergent HA config and never overwrites an existing bound project.

decisions.question: Can display names or normal lifecycle operations break the system binding?
options: Bind stable IDs and protect lifecycle
Treat the hierarchy as a managed system resource.
Identify by names
Find a project by the instance display name on each start.
Ordinary deletable resources
Allow deletion and try to reconstruct later.
decisions.recommendation: A durable instance binding to immutable resource IDs.
decisions.rationale: Names are presentation. A rename must not redirect the running server to another tenant's secrets.
decisions.decision: Allow instance-admin display-name changes. Refuse deletion, moving the active environment, removing system status, changing this project's source-of-truth mode or adding deployment adapters. For this system project, expose one active environment and the runtime-owned schema; custom experiments belong in ordinary projects. Protect all indirect/cascading deletion paths. Do not automatically recreate deleted data. Bind configuration using owner instance ID plus org, project and environment IDs; include the owner in every route/cache key. A root-view entry is a reference, not a centrally stored project. Removing a remote connection removes only the reference and workspace access, never its project or settings. Protect the owning instance’s physical hierarchy from deletion.
decisions.acceptance: Renaming keeps the same binding; direct and parent deletion, import and alternative transport paths cannot bypass lifecycle protection.

decisions.question: Who can change Hikyo's own configuration?
options: Instance administrators
Require instance configuration authority plus the normal scoped capabilities.
System organization administrators
Delegate control through ordinary org/project grants alone.
Any editor
Let normal project write permission control the instance.
decisions.recommendation: Instance-admin access for all system configuration changes.
decisions.rationale: You explicitly approved this boundary because changing these secrets controls Hikyo itself.
decisions.decision: Add an instance-config conjunction to normal operation formulas for the bound hierarchy. Membership administration also requires manage-members at instance scope. Seed the first administrator's scoped grants explicitly. Keep reveal and reveal-history separate; instance-config alone never grants secret disclosure. Revocation takes effect through current transaction-time authorization. For remote projects, evaluate every grant and reauthentication requirement on the owning remote. Local instance-admin or root-view membership conveys no administration rights on another instance.
decisions.acceptance: A principal with only tenant admin grants cannot read, edit, publish, apply or grant access to system configuration.

decisions.question: Where should system-resource protection be enforced?
options: Authorization chokepoint
Resolve the bound resource inside the transaction and enforce its operation formula.
Only hide UI controls
Trust the interface to prevent dangerous operations.
Only the apply endpoint
Protect activation but allow ordinary configuration mutations.
decisions.recommendation: Enforce it centrally, below every transport.
decisions.rationale: API, CLI, imports, schema changes, restore, membership and background work can otherwise become bypasses.
decisions.decision: Define an explicit system-resource operation profile, with a mandatory instance-config conjunct and closed permitted operations. Preserve the additive grant model; do not invent deny grants. Mutation rules cover indirect publication, key classification, linked-key updates and cascading operations. Tenant listings and searches must not expose the system hierarchy to non-admins. Add classification, isolation and operation-formula fixtures before implementation.
decisions.acceptance: A bypass matrix covers UI/API/CLI/MCP, inherited grants, bulk imports, linked keys, schema edits and lifecycle cascades.

decisions.question: How does the server consume its own secrets?
options: Narrow internal runtime authority
A registered worker reads only the bound revision.
Reusable machine token
Store a bearer token and call Hikyo's HTTP API.
Instance-wide secret access
Give the runtime an unrestricted secret reader.
decisions.recommendation: An internal, operation-bound runtime consumer.
decisions.rationale: A self-referential HTTP dependency or expiring human token can stop the server from configuring itself.
decisions.decision: Introduce a specifically registered system authority site for initialization/reconciliation, limited to the immutable instance binding, retained target snapshot and required key operations. Network handlers only authorize and record apply intent; they do not mint a system proof. Runtime authority cannot accept an arbitrary tenant ID or export payload. Audit activation with both initiating principal and executing system site. After durable commit, reconciliation is instance-owned and survives the initiating admin leaving. The runtime consumer is always local to the owning logical instance. It never fetches its config from another Hikyo server or from the root management view.
decisions.acceptance: Forged scopes fail at the store boundary; authority cannot be reused outside its transaction or to read another project's secrets.

decisions.question: Should applying settings require reauthentication or another reviewer?
options: Fresh reauthentication
One authorized admin confirms the exact revision.
Mandatory second approver
Every apply requires another administrator.
Existing session only
No additional assurance at activation.
decisions.recommendation: Target-instance administrator plus fresh passkey or TOTP for Apply.
decisions.rationale: This fits single-operator self-hosting while binding a sensitive instance change to a recent human ceremony.
decisions.decision: The user explicitly requires instance-admin authority with passkey or TOTP authentication. Enforce the owning instance's instance-config capability and an MFA-authenticated human session for protected configuration operations. Adoption, Apply, rollback and test send additionally consume a fresh, single-use passkey or TOTP ceremony bound to the exact owner, revision, schema version and expected generation. Password-only authentication, recovery-code login and machine tokens cannot substitute. Browser and human CLI use the same owner-side enforcement. No mandatory second administrator is introduced. Deployment restoration consumes a distinct rollout-restore action hash bound to the original rollout revision, current generation and exact plan digest. An Apply proof cannot authorize Restore.
decisions.acceptance: Test authorized TOTP and user-verified passkey success, password-only and recovery-only denial, wrong-owner and scoped-admin denial, expired/replayed or revision-mismatched ceremony denial, and direct remote-owner enforcement.

decisions.question: What can leave the system project?
options: Normal encrypted storage, restricted disclosure
Use project encryption and explicit reveal capabilities.
Plaintext instance settings table
Keep values easy to access during boot.
Unlimited integration/export access
Treat system configuration as any ordinary machine workload.
decisions.recommendation: Normal encryption and secret ceremonies, with a closed consumer boundary.
decisions.rationale: Dogfooding must retain real encryption, history and disclosure behavior without turning integrations into an indirect instance-secret export path.
decisions.decision: Store mail passwords as secret cells under the normal project DEK and include them in re-encryption. No plaintext mirror, secret-bearing URL, log, status response or revision diff. Human exports continue to require all normal disclosure permissions plus instance-config; machines, adapters and linked values crossing the system boundary are refused in this delivery. Bound runtime reads do not expose a generic delivery endpoint. Root keys and offline recovery identities are never copied into the project. A remote workspace may return values directly to its authorized human browser using existing disclosure ceremonies. The viewing Hikyo server never proxies, caches or stores remote values. This does not widen directory credentials or add server-to-server secret delivery.
decisions.acceptance: Canary secrets are absent from logs, audit, HTML, errors and unauthorized API results; permitted reveal remains audited.

decisions.question: Which configuration belongs inside Hikyo?
options: Every Hikyo variable, with explicit activation rules
Complete server configuration coverage; classify ordinary activation, node-specific settings and bootstrap transitions.
Original nine-key catalogue
Complete email configuration and release notifications only. This earlier recommendation is superseded.
Import the ambient environment wholesale
Includes unrelated process variables and client credentials; not the meaning of server self-configuration.
decisions.recommendation: Every Hikyo variable, with remote Apply by a target-instance administrator using passkey or TOTP.
decisions.rationale: The user explicitly expanded D11: managing only mail and release notifications does not meet the dogfooding requirement. Each supported server variable needs real activation behavior and recovery semantics, not just an editable entry.
decisions.decision: Supersedes the original nine-key scope. Cover every supported Hikyo server variable, including networking, authentication, endpoint exposure, backup/audit policy and deployment/bootstrap settings. Keep independent remotes in separate projects with target-owner authorization. Shared HA settings and node-specific settings must be distinguished so replicas never receive duplicate node identities. Each variable must declare its effective source, secret classification, validator and activation mechanism. Remote Apply means configuration activation, not the retired binary updater. Client-only variables do not configure a server; retired controls remain explicitly refused. Database and root-key changes require dedicated bootstrap transitions with an independently available unlock source and recovery route. These transition requirements are part of the expanded work, not grounds to silently call the old nine-key implementation complete. Current implementation has 27 top-level keys, including secret HIKYO_NODE_OVERRIDES and alias-only HIKYO_BOOTSTRAP_SOURCES. Ordinary owner/node consumers reload live. The concrete bootstrap provider is limited to an enrolled singleton non-HA Recreate Kubernetes 1.36 deployment; upgrade and HA/node-identity transition families remain acceptance gaps. Other deployment providers are separately scoped platform extensions.
decisions.acceptance: Inventory every recognized variable with no unexplained omissions. Prove each supported change takes effect on its target, survives restart, preserves independent remote values and reports actual HA convergence. Prove database/root-source recovery across failed cutover and process restart, viable authentication after origin changes, and node identity uniqueness. Password-only sessions, recovery codes, machine tokens, wrong-owner privileges and stale/replayed ceremonies cannot authorize Apply.

decisions.question: Which source wins after adoption?
options: Applied revision owns managed keys
External settings seed once and never silently override afterward.
Environment always wins
UI changes may be shadowed by deployment configuration.
Merge on every restart
Resolve missing keys from ambient environment.
decisions.recommendation: One authority per key: the applied revision.
decisions.rationale: A saved email password must not revert when the container restarts.
decisions.decision: Before adoption, retain current startup behavior. After adoption, parse bootstrap settings first and load managed keys exclusively from the durable applied revision. Ignore stale external values for adopted keys with a key-name-only notice, including stale file paths; do not validate or read their file contents. No fallback for absent managed values. Partial mail groups fail validation; an entirely absent group means disabled. Effective defaults become explicit seeded values for settings that have defaults. Source precedence is resolved independently on each owner. There are no root-organization defaults, automatic cross-project links, inherited credentials or remote-variable fallbacks.
decisions.acceptance: Conflicting or malformed stale managed env values and missing old password files cannot shadow or prevent loading a valid applied revision.

decisions.question: How should file-based mail secrets and custom trust be imported?
options: Resolve once during controlled adoption
Import password bytes and custom CA contents into typed managed cells.
Store host file paths in the project
Read arbitrary paths during every apply.
Drop file support
Require operators to re-enter all secrets manually.
decisions.recommendation: Import effective contents, never make remote apply a file-reading interface.
decisions.rationale: A UI-controlled path would let an administrator repurpose the server's filesystem permissions. HA nodes can also have different mounts.
decisions.decision: Only read already configured mail password/CA files through existing startup validation during adoption. Preserve password bytes without trimming. Map PASSWORD_FILE to secret HIKYO_MAIL_PASSWORD and CA_FILE to new configuration HIKYO_MAIL_CA_PEM. Managed mode rejects both *_FILE keys. Reject CA blobs over 64 KiB and malformed or non-certificate PEM material; use the existing cell limit if stricter. Ship no TLS verification bypass. After adoption, later changes to those external files do not change managed configuration. Node TLS and egress sources follow the same one-time import rule: TLS_CERT_PEM, TLS_KEY_PEM and ADAPTER/OIDC/DYNAMIC_EGRESS_POLICY_JSON are canonical fields inside the encrypted node overlay. TLS private-key file import requires 0400 or 0600. Later Apply never reads project-supplied paths.
decisions.acceptance: An API-supplied path cannot read server files; certificate validation is deterministic across nodes and password bytes survive import.

decisions.question: Does Apply need to contact the SMTP server?
options: Validate locally, offer explicit test send
Prepare the client without unsolicited outbound traffic.
Require successful SMTP probe
A relay outage blocks every apply.
Skip mail validation
Let the first real message discover configuration errors.
decisions.recommendation: Local validation plus an explicit test of an exact revision.
decisions.rationale: Hikyo's mail contract prohibits boot-time probes. Network availability and valid configuration are different states.
decisions.decision: Validate required fields, mailbox syntax, TLS policy, custom CA, address and CIDR policy at publish/apply. No DNS/TCP/SMTP dial during boot, adoption or activation. A reauthenticated Test email action may test the selected published candidate or active revision; show which was tested and never treat another revision's success as evidence. Retain #608's 15-second send deadline and 5/hour/principal, 1-concurrent/instance test budget. No recipient chosen or mail sent by this design work.
decisions.acceptance: No-egress tests pass with mail configured; an explicit test sends exactly once and records redacted intent/outcome.

decisions.question: Can users loosen validation or change the system schema?
options: Runtime-owned schema
Expose ordinary schema diagnostics while reserving catalogue edits to the runtime.
Freely editable schema
Let an admin remove constraints to force a publish.
Validate only in the UI
Keep backend handling permissive.
decisions.recommendation: A versioned runtime-owned schema with server-side validation.
decisions.rationale: The matrix should remain familiar, but the contract consumed by Hikyo is defined by the running binary.
decisions.decision: Reject unknown keys, wrong secrecy classification, cross-project references, dynamic-secret values and unsupported key types. A disabled mail group must contain no partial credentials. Every apply revalidates against the current binary's catalogue even when an older snapshot passed its original schema. An upgrade reconciles schema metadata explicitly without rewriting effective values; incompatibility is reported before activation. No schema override for system configuration.
decisions.acceptance: Changing a secret to a public key or using import/restore to inject an unsupported setting fails server-side.

decisions.question: What is the unit of activation?
options: One complete immutable revision
Prepare all affected components, then swap the config bundle.
One key at a time
Mutate global variables incrementally.
Process environment mutation
Call os.Setenv and expect existing components to notice.
decisions.recommendation: One revision and one immutable runtime bundle per process.
decisions.rationale: A mail send must not pair a new username with an old password. Components already constructed from startup config will not update themselves.
decisions.decision: Use a revision-keyed configuration manager; do not use process-env mutation as delivery. Prepare replacement mail client and update-channel consumer without side effects, then swap the whole bundle atomically. Each operation captures one bundle for its lifetime. A send admitted before the swap may complete with the old bundle within its existing deadline; new sends use the new bundle. Retire old resources after their users finish. The expanded supervisor replaces the authentication, federation, MCP, proxy, backup, audit and egress graph while retaining datastore/keyring identity. It reserves changed sockets, drains requests and workers, preserves admission counters, activates PostgreSQL pool changes and installs TLS contents before acknowledgement. The original nine mail/channel keys avoid unnecessary graph rebuilds.
decisions.acceptance: Concurrency/race tests prove each operation uses a single revision and that invalid candidates never partially modify a live bundle.

decisions.question: How do concurrent applies and crash recovery behave?
options: Durable generation and idempotent job
Serialize applies using expected-generation checks and a recorded target.
Last request wins
Allow one administrator to unknowingly replace another's apply.
Memory-only activation
Persist success after swapping and hope the process survives.
decisions.recommendation: A durable apply job and compare-and-swap generation.
decisions.rationale: Database commits and in-memory swaps cannot be a single transaction. Their boundary must be recoverable.
decisions.decision: Resolve an exact retained snapshot; validate/preflight; recheck initiating authority before committing desired generation, retention roots and an apply intent atomically. Repeated requests with the same idempotency key and same request return the same job; a changed request conflicts. Before durable commit, any failure preserves the old target. After commit, nodes reconcile that target and report pending/partial until acknowledged. A crash between commit and swap resumes on restart; it is never reported as 'old config guaranteed unchanged'. Scope the job, idempotency key, generation, snapshot and revision to the immutable owning instance/project/environment tuple. Revision r13 on one remote is unrelated to r13 elsewhere. A target switch or changed remote identity invalidates the prepared action rather than retargeting it. An explicitly failed or timed-out committed target may be superseded by a published repair revision. Repair preparation keeps the failed target committed and business work fenced; only fresh exact MFA commits the replacement. The old job remains visible as superseded. Preparing or actively converging jobs remain single-flight. A partial bootstrap rollout cannot be superseded while the executor has a nonterminal plan. Restore deployment first, using separate exact MFA and a durable signed command, then wait for verified Restored before a new repair Apply. Restore keeps the target fenced and does not change the desired revision.
decisions.acceptance: Fault injection at every commit/swap boundary yields a recoverable target; concurrent stale-generation requests return conflicts without side effects.

decisions.question: What does Apply mean for HA replicas versus independent remotes?
options: Coordinated preparation and per-node acknowledgement
Fence stale consumers and report convergence honestly.
Only reload the serving node
Other nodes pick it up eventually with no status.
Promise an instantaneous global swap
Hide the distributed transition from operators.
decisions.recommendation: A fenced generation with visible node convergence.
decisions.rationale: A UI request may hit any replica. Local atomicity does not provide global atomicity.
decisions.decision: Use the existing PostgreSQL node registry and fenced coordination. Preflight every admitted serving node against the candidate and catalogue version; an unready/incompatible participant blocks commit. Fix membership for the preparation generation and fence late joiners until they reconcile. After commit, each node swaps locally and acknowledges the generation. Before starting affected operations, stale nodes must reconcile or refuse with a retryable unavailable response; readiness also reports stale status. In-flight operations already admitted may finish with their captured revision. Keep administration and recovery reachable. No-success-on-quorum shortcut. The participant set contains only HA replicas of the selected logical instance, sharing its database and root-key authority. Configured remotes are never members of this barrier and never receive this apply. Do not infer HA membership from equal names, versions, variables or origins.
decisions.acceptance: Two-node HA tests cover partial failure, mixed binaries, leader death, late nodes and stale direct traffic. With two independent remotes using different SMTP values, applying to either changes only its own HA replicas; unrelated remote outages cannot block it.

decisions.question: What status and bounds should operators see?
options: Explicit phase and revision status
Show preparing, applying, applied, failed or partial plus affected nodes.
One success toast
Report success when the API accepted the request.
Raw logs only
Ask operators to inspect each process.
decisions.recommendation: An asynchronous job with honest status.
decisions.rationale: Long-running activation must survive a browser refresh and must distinguish acceptance from observed completion.
decisions.decision: Expose desired revision, per-node active revision, last completed job, timestamp and secret-safe errors. If nodes differ, report mixed state rather than one global active revision. Proposed first-delivery bounds: 1 apply job per instance, 10 new applies/minute/instance, a five-minute preparation/review TTL, at most 30 seconds waiting per request, and a 30-second post-commit convergence deadline and a 2-second reconciliation poll. Preparation expiry aborts without commit. Post-commit expiry reports partial and keeps reconciling; do not auto-rollback. Bound and test these constants; duplicate idempotent retries do not consume a new apply budget. Always display the owning instance identity/name and project beside revision/status. Poll job state directly on that owner through the existing workspace session. An unreachable remote is unknown/offline with a last-observed timestamp, never implicitly in sync with local state. Final commitment rechecks worker timestamps against the transaction clock: future timestamps and attestations 30 seconds old or older are refused. Status ready-to-authorize is not a substitute for this final check.
decisions.acceptance: Closing/reopening the browser recovers the job; a missing node never produces a green Applied state. Unsupported or unacknowledged nodes stay visibly named.

decisions.question: Does a failed relay connection undo an applied revision?
options: Keep config and show delivery failure
Let the administrator test, edit or roll back deliberately.
Automatically switch old credentials back on
Treat any SMTP failure as bad configuration.
Stop the whole app
Fail all requests when email is unavailable.
decisions.recommendation: Separate configuration activation from delivery health.
decisions.rationale: An SMTP outage does not prove the new settings are wrong. Silent rollback might reactivate a retired credential.
decisions.decision: Validation/preparation failure prevents commit. Delivery failure after activation records an explicit failed send and keeps the active revision. Existing mail-dependent operations follow #608's refusal and resend contracts; browsing and admin repair remain available. Do not introduce a new mail retry outbox or duplicate sends. Release-channel changes affect notification polling only; they do not enable remote software upgrades.
decisions.acceptance: An unreachable relay produces a visible failure without changing active revision or automatically retrying a test message.

decisions.question: How does rollback work?
options: Restore, publish and apply through normal history
Revalidate old values against the current catalogue.
Rewrite the active snapshot
Mutate historical content.
Silently select any older revision
Bypass current validation or historical permissions.
decisions.recommendation: Use normal restore and publication, then explicit apply.
decisions.rationale: Hikyo's existing history already makes rollback reviewable and validates against the current schema.
decisions.decision: Restore a previous configuration into drafts, preserve unrelated drafts, preview, publish a new immutable revision and apply it. Require normal restore/publish/history authority plus instance-config and fresh activation reauthentication. A UI shortcut may guide the sequence but must retain its review boundaries. Local recovery can select a retained revision directly only after current-catalogue validation, with an audited generation change and no schema override. History and rollback are owner-local. A revision from another project or instance is not a rollback candidate. External deployment restoration is separate: Restore deployment sends a freshly authorized exact retained-plan rollback. The controller must confirm Restored; only a later published repair with fresh Apply MFA can resume configuration. No automatic rollback or automatic root finalization is selected.
decisions.acceptance: Rollback creates new lineage; tightened validation rejects obsolete settings with named fields instead of bypassing the schema.

decisions.question: What prevents garbage collection of the running config?
options: Bounded, explicit runtime retention roots
Protect the desired, node-active and recovery revisions.
Ordinary expiring workload pin
Risk the running payload expiring while the process remains healthy.
Disable all retention
Keep every secret revision forever.
decisions.recommendation: A first-class runtime retention reference with a narrow lifecycle.
decisions.rationale: An applied revision can stop being the latest published snapshot, and normal pins have finite lifetimes.
decisions.decision: Amend retention explicitly: protect the desired snapshot, every snapshot still used by an admitted node or unfinished job, and the previous completed activation for recovery. Acquire/release these references under the same snapshot/GC locks as publication. Serialize applies. A partial target may be replaced through explicit repair preparation while retaining the desired target, previous completed target and one candidate. Supersede the old partial job metadata without committing the repair until preparation and fresh exact MFA pass. Keep at most three distinct runtime-referenced payloads in steady single-flight operation. Stale nodes are fenced before their references are released; they cannot resume an old generation. Surface retained-by-runtime in history, then return released payloads to normal retention. Never recycle a normal pin into a hidden infinite pin. Retention roots and GC are confined to the owning instance; no root-view reference retains or copies another instance’s payload. For bootstrap partial jobs, release/supersede the external operation only after verified Applied or Restored terminal evidence. Preserve the previous completed activation while repairing a failed target.
decisions.acceptance: GC racing apply/rollback cannot collect required payloads; hundreds of completed applies do not retain hundreds of system revisions.

decisions.question: How can an operator recover when the UI cannot start?
options: Explicit host-local recovery
Inspect metadata and select a retained valid revision while writers are fenced.
Ambient environment override
Silently let deployment variables replace stored configuration.
Database edits by hand
Repair internal rows without authorization or audit.
decisions.recommendation: A documented host-local recovery command.
decisions.rationale: Self-management needs an escape hatch outside the managed configuration, without an invisible second source of truth.
decisions.decision: Use the existing local-authority/recovery framework with external DB/root-key access. Command family: hikyo admin config status and hikyo admin config recover --revision <n>. Require a quiesced single writer, or a cluster-wide fence; validate payload, preserve recovery restrictions and record the new generation plus recovery audit. An invalid committed config must never silently fall back to process env. A removed/invalid catalogue key fails before affected runtime use; health and local recovery explain the cause. Run recovery on the affected owning instance. The viewing instance’s root screen is not an offline recovery authority for a disconnected remote.
decisions.acceptance: A broken applied revision is repaired without manual SQL, access to the public UI, plaintext secret output or competing HA writers.

decisions.question: What happens after backup restore or key rotation?
options: Preserve encrypted state and reauthorize recovery
Restore binding/history but keep outbound use fenced until reconciliation.
Send immediately with restored credentials
Trust a historical backup to reactivate external access.
Discard all managed config
Force a fresh installation after every restore.
decisions.recommendation: Integrate with the existing encryption and recovery lifecycle.
decisions.rationale: Persisting SMTP credentials in Hikyo changes their backup/restore posture; the current mail spec assumes process-owned credentials.
decisions.decision: Backups include the binding, schema, encrypted cells, retained payloads and durable activation state. Existing key rotation/re-encryption must cover these as project secrets. After restore, use the new recovery incarnation to invalidate stale acknowledgements, pause mail and other outbound self-config consumers, reconcile grants under the existing recovery procedure and require credential confirmation or re-entry plus explicit apply before resuming. Do not assert that old SMTP credentials remain valid. Audit this resumption separately. HA restores preserve one logical instance binding. A restored clone running alongside its source is an identity collision, not a new remote or HA member; retain the existing multi-instance refusal until an explicit supported identity separation occurs. The apply form records an explicit credential-and-grant review confirmation after restore, bound into the exact reauthentication target and separately audited on resumption.
decisions.acceptance: Restore drills prove no outbound mail before reconciliation and explicit resumption, on SQLite and PostgreSQL; key rotation preserves readable configuration without leakage.

decisions.question: How should this design become shipped behavior?
options: Amend contracts and deliver verified slices
Integrate with the existing mailer work and require end-to-end proof.
Build a parallel SMTP implementation
Bypass the pending mailer specification.
Call the report implementation complete
Treat design approval as a working feature.

decisions.question: Do independent remote instances share configuration?
options: One project per logical instance
Independent instances own separate schemas, values and revisions; HA replicas share their instance’s project.
One project with an environment per remote
Separate some values but assume a shared key catalogue and publication domain.
One shared configuration for all instances
Propagate the same variables to every connected server.
decisions.recommendation: Separate projects for independent instances; shared project only within an HA instance.
decisions.rationale: You explicitly clarified that remote instances cannot be assumed to share variables. An environment per remote would still couple their key catalogues; projects preserve the full boundary.
decisions.decision: Treat an instance as the ownership and activation unit. Every independent instance has its own system project, schema, secrets, drafts, history, applied generation, retention and recovery state. HA replicas share their one logical instance’s project and active revision; node-specific bootstrap settings remain external. Do not introduce inherited root values, automatic copies or cross-instance fan-out. Same variable names may have different values or be absent independently.
decisions.acceptance: Use two remotes with different SMTP hosts/passwords and supported keys plus an HA pair on one remote. Applying to that pair updates both replicas and none of the other remote’s state. Identical display names/revision numbers do not merge targets; an offline remote does not block another owner’s apply.

decisions.question: Should the root organization physically store every remote’s configuration?
options: One root management view, local ownership
Group per-instance project references in one place while each remote stores and serves its own configuration.
One central physical organization
Store every instance’s configuration on a designated central server and distribute it.
Separate navigation with no root view
Keep ownership isolated but make users switch interfaces to find each project.
decisions.recommendation: One Hikyo root management view; a protected physical organization remains on each owner.
decisions.rationale: The proposed root grouping is useful, but a single physical org spanning databases would introduce central state management and a cross-instance secret/boot dependency. The existing remote architecture explicitly preserves owner-local state and browser-direct access.
decisions.decision: Interpret root as an aggregation in the management interface, not a new global tenant, super-admin scope or central secret store. Each owner retains its protected Hikyo organization and instance-named project. The root shows local and remote project references with an explicit owning instance/origin. Resolve configuration metadata and apply operations through the remote’s authenticated human workspace API; directory credentials retain metadata-only authority. Without owner-side access, show a sign-in/access state rather than assuming permission. Connecting/disconnecting a remote changes navigation only. No central main instance is introduced, no server proxies or copies another server’s secrets, and loss of the viewing instance does not interrupt remote boot or runtime configuration. A physical central root organization would be a separate change to the locked multi-instance contract, not an unstated consequence of this recommendation.
decisions.acceptance: Prove browser-to-owner requests, owner-local audit and owner-admin checks. An admin on the viewer without remote authority cannot reveal/edit/apply there. Disconnecting the viewer leaves the remote operational and its local project intact. Label the root as a management group so it cannot be mistaken for a shared physical organization.

decisions.question: Which deployment can bootstrap Apply control in this implementation?
options: Explicitly enrolled singleton Kubernetes
Start with one non-HA Recreate deployment, stable node identity, fixed resources and Kubernetes 1.36 admission enforcement.
Host and GitOps providers together
Requires additional durable source writers, authority and recovery implementations.
Assume every deployment can be patched

decisions.rationale: Bootstrap source authority must survive pod replacement and must not be silently overwritten by another controller. The available implementation uses a signed metadata mailbox and fixed-resource executor.
decisions.decision: The concrete provider accepts one non-HA stable-node Recreate deployment under explicit enrollment and Kubernetes 1.36 admission controls. Operator provisioning must install custody, source aliases, resource UIDs, signer trust and mutation restrictions. Host/GitOps providers and HA bootstrap transitions are not implemented. This limit does not narrow the user’s complete-server-variable objective or make that objective complete. Durable exact-authorized commands renew their transport sequence and timestamps after an executor outage without changing the authorized plan. Preparation cannot acquire renewal authority. Local renewal/no-effect restoration tests and R2 review pass; actual cluster transport-expiry recovery now passes; executor process-death/takeover was not exercised.

decisions.question: How is a partially applied bootstrap deployment repaired?
options: Explicit Restore, then separate repair Apply
Use fresh exact MFA for each decision and keep the desired runtime fenced between them.
Automatically roll back
Could undo a deliberate source transition without a current administrator decision.
Supersede the unfinished controller plan
Would strand the old external operation and block later rollouts.
decisions.recommendation: Restore deployment resources explicitly, then authorize a configuration repair separately.
decisions.rationale: External resource restoration and application activation are different facts. Neither a successful HTTP request nor a Restored receipt proves the desired app revision is usable.
decisions.decision: A target instance administrator authorizes rollout-restore for the original job revision, current generation and plan digest. The final transaction spends that proof once and records a signed Restore command plus audit. A worker sends it. Capture immediately fences business work; controller-confirmed Restored enables a new repair preparation. The separately published repair needs fresh Apply MFA. The desired revision never changes merely because restoration was requested.
decisions.acceptance: Both engines must reject Apply proofs, changed plans/generations and journal races without spending the valid restore proof; idempotent retries send no new decision. Prove Restore → fresh repair → a later bootstrap rollout.

decisions.question: What prevents a public-origin change from stranding passkey administrators?
options: Require origin-independent recovery credentials
For a changed RP hostname, require fresh TOTP and a current password credential on the same account.
Accept an existing passkey alone
Its RP binding may not work at the proposed hostname.
Treat an origin string as reachability proof
Would not establish DNS, TLS, routing or a successful login.
decisions.recommendation: Require the implemented TOTP/password recovery path and retain target-origin verification as an acceptance gap.
decisions.rationale: A passkey is scoped to an RP hostname. A health response or syntactically valid origin does not prove an administrator can authenticate there.
decisions.decision: The actual last-installed origin is retained independently of runtime availability. Changing its RP hostname requires an exact fresh TOTP decision plus live confirmed TOTP and current password credentials for the same initiating administrator. Same-host port changes may use passkeys. Host-local recovery remains independent. This does not prove remembered password knowledge or new-origin network access.
decisions.acceptance: Both engines cover wrong account, stale epoch, removed factors, changed host and same-host changes. A real target-origin access ceremony or operational verification remains outstanding.

decisions.question: How should development-only variables become remotely manageable?

Allow Apply to enable development mode

decisions.rationale: The environment controls are requested settings. The deployment trust domain is a separate startup choice, and provider changes must not redirect existing effects.
decisions.decision: Accepted using the user’s standing approval of recommendations. The integrated implementation manages all three controls only for an existing development deployment. Production rejects their presence. Limiter and budget counters survive changes; simulated provider state survives reload. Unsafe real/fake provider changes refuse before installation and are rechecked after runtime drain. Focused tests, race checks, lint, vet and independent R1 review pass. decisions.decision: Accepted using the user’s standing approval of recommendations. The integrated implementation selects or clears an enrolled candidate through exact-MFA Apply. Initial, saved and missing-node candidate health validates source availability before startup admission. Focused runtime/rotation tests, race checks, vet and R3 review pass.
